title: The Envelope Has Four Jobs: Water, Air, Vapour and Heat
summary: The building envelope separates inside from outside by controlling four things in order of importance: liquid water, air, water vapour and heat. In a hot-humid climate the vapour drive runs from the outside in, which reverses rules written for cold climates. The owner who knows the four layers can ask where each one is and whether it is continuous.
body:
The envelope has four jobs, in order of importance: keep rain out, keep air from leaking through, manage water vapour, and slow the flow of heat. Each job needs a continuous layer, and in a hot-humid climate the vapour job runs backwards from the rules most textbooks teach.

Recall

Q. What is a statement of special inspections?

A. The permit document listing which critical work will be specially inspected, how often and by whom; the owner usually engages the agency directly.

Q. What is the difference between active and passive fire protection?

A. Active protection must operate when a fire starts, such as sprinklers and alarms; passive protection works by being intact, such as rated walls, doors and firestopping.

Q. In the wealth post-mortems, what is a currency mismatch?

A. Earning income in one currency while owing debts or spending in another, so a movement in the exchange rate can turn a solvent position into a shortfall without any change in the underlying business.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the envelope is the part of a building most likely to generate claims after completion. Leaks, mould, failed sealants, peeling finishes and high cooling bills almost always trace back to the envelope, and they arrive after the contractor has left and the warranty clock is running. In a condominium they arrive as a claim from an owners' association. In a rental they arrive as lost rent and a damaged reputation. Most of them are decided in design, at the junctions between systems, long before anything is built.

The four control layers

In plain English, an exterior wall or roof has to do four things. Stop liquid water, such as rain, from getting in, and drain out what does get in. Stop air from leaking through, because moving air carries moisture and heat with it. Manage water vapour, the invisible moisture in air, so it does not condense inside the wall. And slow the flow of heat so the building is comfortable and cheap to cool.

The professional framing calls these the four control layers, and building scientists rank them in that order: water first, then air, then vapour, then heat. The ranking matters because owners and designers often spend most attention on insulation, the fourth job, while most failures come from the first two. Each layer must be continuous: across the wall, around every window and door, through every penetration and at every transition from wall to roof, wall to slab and one material to another. A layer that is perfect in the middle of the wall and broken at the window is broken.

Hot-humid: the vapour drive runs inward

Water vapour moves from warm, moist air toward cooler, drier air. In a cold climate, the inside is warm and moist in winter, so vapour drives outward, and designers put a vapour retarder on the warm, interior side. In a hot-humid climate, the outside is hot and humid nearly all year and the inside is air-conditioned, so the drive runs inward. A layer that stops vapour on the inside face, such as vinyl wallcovering or certain impermeable paints, traps moisture inside the wall where it meets the cool back of the interior finish.

The professional term is vapour drive: the direction and strength of vapour movement through an assembly, set by the difference in vapour pressure across it. In hot-humid design, the rules are to keep the air barrier continuous, keep impermeable layers off the interior face, let the wall dry toward the inside, and keep the building slightly pressurised with dry, conditioned air so humid outdoor air is not pulled in through gaps.

Worked example: the hotel room wall

Hypothetically, an apart-hotel in a hot-humid coastal climate finishes its guest rooms with vinyl wallcovering on the exterior walls, because it is durable and easy to clean. The wall behind it has a gap in the air barrier at each floor slab. Humid outdoor air leaks in through the gap, travels up the stud cavity and reaches the back of the gypsum board, which is cooled by the room air conditioning. Its temperature is below the dew point of the outdoor air, so water condenses. The vinyl stops it drying into the room. Within a year, mould grows behind the wallcovering, the rooms smell, and guests complain.

Two changes would have prevented it: a continuous air barrier sealed at every slab edge, and a vapour-permeable interior finish so the wall could dry inward. Neither is expensive at design. Both are very expensive after occupancy, when every room must be stripped.

Say that out loud now.

In a hot-humid climate the vapour drives inward. Seal the air, and keep impermeable finishes off the inside face.

Worked example: the window that is only as good as its installation

A window can be rated and tested in a laboratory and still leak in the wall. Water most often enters not through the glass or the frame but around it, at the rough opening. The control is a sloped sill pan with end dams that collects any water and drains it to the outside, flashing lapped so that each upper layer overlaps the one below like shingles, and an air seal between the frame and the air barrier. The rule designers use is that water should always run down and out, over each layer, never behind it.

Glazing and roofs in one paragraph each

Glazing is the envelope's weakest thermal layer and its biggest source of solar heat. Two numbers describe it: the U-factor, how fast heat flows through, and the solar heat gain coefficient, how much of the sun's heat passes. In a hot climate the second usually matters more. In a hurricane region, impact resistance is a separate requirement, as Ravi and Bram taught in Week 99.

Roofs fail at edges, penetrations and low spots. A roof needs positive slope to drains, often by tapered insulation, edges and copings designed for wind uplift, and every penetration flashed and kept away from drains and corners where possible.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: envelope replacement may be treated as a repair or as a capital improvement depending on its scope and the system's rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: envelope defects are the classic source of latent-defect claims after completion, so contracts must allocate design and installation responsibility at every junction. Banking: a lender's monitor and insurer will want evidence of field testing before completion. Governance: one party, usually an envelope consultant, should own the continuity of each control layer across trades. Estate: envelope warranties and test records are long-life documents that pass with the asset. Exit: a buyer's property condition assessment will look for leaks, mould and sealant failure, and price them.

Professional sign-off required: architect of record, for the envelope design; building enclosure consultant, for continuity and testing; mechanical engineer, for pressurisation and dehumidification.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that each trade installs its own part of the envelope correctly and nobody owns the junctions between them, where water, air and vapour actually get in. The control is a building enclosure consultant who reviews the transition details, a mock-up tested before production, and field testing during construction.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner copies an envelope detail from a cold-climate project or a manufacturer's generic brochure, with a vapour retarder on the inside face. In a hot-humid climate, that detail can trap moisture in every wall. Ask which way the vapour drives on your site before you approve the wall section.

Callback

In Week 98, Zara and Cade taught that design management is largely the management of interfaces between consultants' scopes, and that gaps between scopes are where errors live. The envelope is the physical version of that lesson: the gap between the window installer's scope and the air barrier installer's scope is a literal gap in the wall.

Recap

The envelope controls water, air, vapour and heat, in that order of importance, and each layer must be continuous through every junction. In a hot-humid climate the vapour drive runs inward, so seal the air and keep impermeable finishes off the interior face. Windows leak at their installation, and roofs at their edges and penetrations.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: the Grenfell Tower fire of 2017 and what it teaches about envelope products.
checklist: I know where each of the four control layers is in every wall and roof section.
Every control layer is continuous at windows, slabs, roof edges and penetrations.
I know which way the vapour drives on my site.
No impermeable finish is specified on the interior face in a hot-humid climate.
Windows have sloped sill pans, end dams and shingle-lapped flashing.
The building is designed to be slightly pressurised with dry air.
A building enclosure consultant reviews every transition detail.
A full-size mock-up is tested before production.
head: Field checklist
speak: The building envelope has four jobs, in order of importance: keep liquid water out and drain what gets in; stop air leaking through; manage water vapour so it does not condense inside the wall; and slow heat flow. Each needs a continuous layer through every junction, at windows, slab edges, roof edges and penetrations, because that is where failures start. In a hot-humid climate, vapour drives from the hot, humid outside toward the air-conditioned inside, which reverses cold-climate rules. So I keep the air barrier continuous, keep impermeable finishes such as vinyl wallcovering off the interior face, let the wall dry inward and keep the building slightly pressurised with dry air. Windows leak around their installation, so they need sloped sill pans, end dams and shingle-lapped flashing. Roofs fail at edges, drains and penetrations. One envelope consultant owns the junctions, with a tested mock-up and field testing.
terms: Control layer — a continuous layer in a wall or roof that controls one of water, air, vapour or heat.
Vapour drive — the direction and strength of water vapour movement through an assembly, set by the vapour pressure difference across it.
Dew point — the temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapour begins to condense on a surface.

hostile.q: This is a coastal hot-humid site and your wall section shows vinyl wallcovering on the exterior walls. Why is that not a mould claim waiting to happen?
hostile.a: It would be, so we are changing it. In this climate the vapour drives inward, so an impermeable interior finish traps moisture. The revised section uses a vapour-permeable interior finish, a continuous air barrier sealed at every slab edge and window, and mechanical pressurisation with dehumidified air. The enclosure consultant has reviewed the revised details and we will test the air barrier on the mock-up before production.

title: Grenfell Tower: The Envelope That Carried the Fire
summary: On 14 June 2017, a fire in a flat at Grenfell Tower in London spread up the building's newly refurbished exterior and killed 72 people. The inquiry's final report in 2024 found failures across government, manufacturers, testing bodies, designers, contractors and the building's managers. Seven forensic steps, with Cole on integrity, show how an envelope product chosen on cost and certificates became the path of the fire.
body:
At Grenfell Tower, the fire did not spread through the building; it spread up its skin. A refurbishment added an envelope that carried fire, chosen through a chain of certificates, assumptions and, the inquiry found, dishonest product claims that nobody in the chain tested.

Recall

Q. How do you run a rough gravity load takedown?

A. Tributary area times dead and live load per floor, factored by the governing combination, added floor by floor, with units beside every number.

Q. What happened at the MGM Grand fire in 1980?

A. A fire in a ground-floor restaurant area spread through an unsprinklered casino, and smoke rose into the hotel tower through vertical openings, killing 85 people, most from smoke.

Q. What is concentration risk on a personal balance sheet?

A. Too large a share of wealth in one asset, market or counterparty, so a single adverse event damages the whole position.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is a British case, and British regulations differ from American ones. The lesson is not about the rules of one country. It is about how an owner, a designer and a contractor select envelope products, and about the difference between a product certificate and the proven behaviour of a whole assembly in a fire. Cole joins me because the inquiry found that dishonesty by some product manufacturers was part of the chain, and an owner needs to know how to protect himself from claims he cannot verify personally.

The facts below come from the public record and the reports of the Grenfell Tower Inquiry. Where I describe motives, that is interpretation, not finding.

1. Timeline

Grenfell Tower was a residential tower in North Kensington, west London, built in the 1970s and owned by the local council, with a management organisation running it. A refurbishment completed in 2016 added new windows and an external rainscreen of aluminium composite material panels with a polyethylene core, over combustible foam insulation. Shortly before one o'clock in the morning on 14 June 2017, a fire began in a fridge-freezer in a flat on a lower floor. It escaped through the window area into the new cladding and spread rapidly up and around the exterior. Residents had been advised to stay in their flats, the usual strategy for a building designed to contain fire within each flat, and that advice remained in place long after the exterior fire had defeated the compartments. Seventy-two people died. The inquiry's first report was published in October 2019 and its final report on 4 September 2024.

2. Key decisions

The decisive choices were made in the refurbishment: which cladding panel, which insulation, and which details at windows and cavities. The inquiry found that the panel specified was changed to a cheaper version during procurement, and that the combination installed was highly combustible. A further decision, the building's fire strategy of staying put, had been sound for the original concrete building and was not reconsidered after the envelope changed.

3. Assumptions

Each party assumed the products were safe because of what they had been told: certificates, marketing literature and test claims. Designers assumed the contractor had checked compliance; contractors assumed the designers had; the client assumed its professionals had. The fire strategy assumed the exterior could not carry fire from flat to flat.

4. Incentives

The refurbishment was under cost pressure, and the cheaper panel saved money. Manufacturers had commercial incentives to present their products as suitable for tall buildings. Cole's point is this: when a product claim is the only thing standing between your building and a catastrophic failure, the incentives of the party making the claim are part of your risk, and the inquiry found that some manufacturers had misled the market about how their products behaved in fire.

Say that out loud now.

A certificate tells me what someone claims. A test of the whole assembly, as built, tells me what it does.

5. Warning signs ignored

The inquiry found that the dangers of combustible cladding on tall buildings had been known in the industry and to government for years, including from earlier fires elsewhere, and that warnings had not led to effective action. On the project itself, the change to a cheaper panel was a warning sign: any substitution in a life-safety element deserves a fresh check that it is still safe, not only that it is cheaper.

6. Point of no return

For the building, the point of no return was the installation of the combustible envelope without a test of the assembly. For the residents on the night, it came when the exterior fire spread faster than the strategy of staying in flats could cope with, and the advice was not changed in time.

7. Root cause

The inquiry identified failures across government, the regulatory guidance, manufacturers, testing and certification bodies, designers, contractors, the council and the management organisation. From an owner's seat, the root cause can be put simply: a combustible exterior was put on a residential tower because every party relied on someone else's paper rather than on proven performance of the assembly as built.

Cole's view: protecting yourself from claims you cannot check

You cannot personally test every product. You can set rules that make dishonest or careless claims harder to rely on. Require the governing fire test for the whole wall assembly, not for one component. Require that the product installed is the product tested, with any substitution re-approved in writing by the architect and fire engineer. Keep submittals, test reports and delivery records together. And ask the question an auditor asks: if this certificate were false, what else would tell me?

The American frame

In the United States, the International Building Code limits combustible materials in exterior walls of certain construction types and heights, and refers to NFPA 285, a large-scale test of how fire spreads on an exterior wall assembly with combustible components; verify against the current adopted edition. The details differ from British rules, but the principle is the same: the assembly is tested, not the panel alone.

What an owner of a much smaller building should take from it

It is tempting to think this is a lesson only for towers. The same chain, a cheaper substitute, a certificate in place of a test and a fire strategy nobody revisited, can appear on a mid-rise apartment building, an apart-hotel or a retail podium with residences above. Whenever the exterior wall carries combustible material, insulation, a weather barrier, a cladding core or a balcony finish, ask the fire protection engineer to confirm in writing that the assembly as built is permitted for the construction type and height, and that the fire strategy still holds.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is selecting and substituting envelope products on certificates, data sheets and assurances, without proof that the assembly as built passes the governing fire test. The control is a specification that names the tested assembly, a substitution rule that requires written re-approval by the architect and fire protection engineer, and records tying the delivered product to the tested one.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats cladding as an aesthetic and cost choice. On any building where people sleep, the exterior wall is also part of the fire strategy, and the fire engineer must approve it.

Callback

Last week's Rule 103 said a structural change needs the engineer of record's written confirmation that the load path still works. Grenfell is the same rule in the envelope: a substitution in a life-safety element needs a fresh, written check that the fire strategy still works, not only a cheaper price.

Recap

A refurbishment gave Grenfell Tower a combustible exterior; a kitchen fire spread up it; the stay-put strategy was not changed in time; 72 people died. The inquiry found failures across the whole system, including dishonest product claims. The owner's defence is to require tested assemblies, control substitutions and keep the records.

Rule 104: Never accept an envelope product on a certificate or a component test; require proof that the whole assembly, as built, passes the governing fire test, and re-approve every substitution in writing.

Next: Sage on The Money: what the envelope costs, and what its failures cost later.
checklist: The exterior wall is reviewed by the fire protection engineer as part of the fire strategy.
The specification names the tested wall assembly, not only the products.
Every envelope substitution is re-approved in writing by the architect and fire engineer.
The delivered product is tied to the tested product by records.
I ask what else would tell me if a certificate were false.
The fire strategy is reconsidered whenever the envelope changes.
Submittals, test reports and delivery records are kept together.
head: Field checklist
speak: On 14 June 2017, a fire in a flat at Grenfell Tower in London escaped into the building's newly refurbished exterior: aluminium composite panels with a polyethylene core over combustible insulation. It spread up and around the outside, residents were told to stay in their flats long after the compartments had failed, and 72 people died. The inquiry's final report, published on 4 September 2024, found failures across government, guidance, manufacturers, testing and certification bodies, designers, contractors, the council and the managers, including dishonest product claims. The owner's lesson is the difference between a certificate and proven performance. In the United States, combustible exterior walls are controlled by the building code with NFPA 285 testing of the whole assembly. Rule 104: never accept an envelope product on a certificate or a component test; require proof that the whole assembly, as built, passes the governing fire test, and re-approve every substitution in writing.
terms: Aluminium composite material — a cladding panel of two thin aluminium sheets bonded to a core, which may be combustible depending on the core.
Rainscreen — an outer cladding layer with a ventilated, drained cavity behind it that protects the wall from rain.
Stay put strategy — a fire strategy in which residents remain in their flats because construction is meant to contain a fire within one flat.

hostile.q: Your contractor proposes a different cladding panel that is 15 percent cheaper and has the same certificate. Why should we not take it?
hostile.a: Because a certificate is not a test of our wall. The substitute will be considered only if the manufacturer shows the whole assembly, with our insulation, sheathing, cavity and fixings, has passed the governing fire test, and if the architect and fire protection engineer re-approve it in writing. If that evidence exists, we will look at the saving. If it does not, we keep the specified assembly.

rule: Rule 104: Never accept an envelope product on a certificate or a component test; require proof that the whole assembly, as built, passes the governing fire test, and re-approve every substitution in writing.

title: What the Envelope Costs, and What Its Failures Cost Later
summary: The envelope is a large share of hard cost, but its most important cost is the one that arrives after completion: leaks, mould, energy and replacement. A small spend on mock-ups, testing and an enclosure consultant is cheap insurance against claims that hit NOI, value and reputation. Price the envelope over its life, not at tender.
body:
An envelope is priced at tender and paid for over its whole life. The money that matters most is not the cladding rate but the cost of leaks, mould, cooling and early replacement, which a small spend on testing and review can prevent.

Recall

Q. Why should an owner never release procurement before a substitution is approved?

A. Because once an order is placed, the cost of saying no rises every day and pressure to accept moves to the owner; commitment must not run ahead of approval.

Q. Why does a fire pump drive cost beyond the pump itself?

A. Because it may need standby power, fuel storage and protected rooms that take rentable area.

Q. What is custody risk in personal wealth?

A. The risk that the party holding your assets loses, misuses or steals them, which is why segregation, independent statements and verification matter.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, envelope failures are slow and expensive. A wall that leaks a little in its first year may not show damage for three. By then, the contractor's warranty may be near its end, the trades have moved on, and the owner pays to open walls, dry structure, remove mould and reinstate finishes while tenants or guests are displaced. In a condominium, the claim comes from owners who are also your buyers' neighbours and references. This lesson puts those risks into the numbers.

The cost at tender

In plain English, the envelope is everything between inside and outside: walls, cladding, windows, doors, roofs and their seals. In a mid-rise residential building it is commonly one of the largest trade packages after structure. The professional framing divides it into the systems themselves and the work at their junctions. The systems are bought by area. The junctions are where the risk is, and they are often underpriced because they fall between trades.

Worked example: the mock-up and the testing budget

All figures are hypothetical round numbers. A building has 60,000 square feet of exterior wall, priced at 90 dollars per square foot, or 5,400,000 dollars. The owner adds three items: a building enclosure consultant at 120,000 dollars for design review and site visits; a full-size performance mock-up, tested for water and air before production, at 80,000 dollars; and field testing of installed windows and air barrier during construction at 60,000 dollars. The total is 260,000 dollars, about 4.8 percent of the wall cost.

Now the alternative. Suppose that without those controls, a sill flashing defect repeats on 20 percent of 400 windows. Repairing each, including opening the wall, drying, mould removal and reinstating finishes, costs a hypothetical 6,000 dollars, so 80 windows cost 480,000 dollars. Add consultants and legal costs to establish cause, say 100,000 dollars, and lost rent while units are repaired, say 80 units out for three weeks at 2,000 dollars a month, about 120,000 dollars. The failure costs about 700,000 dollars, nearly three times the prevention, before any reputational cost.

Say that out loud now.

The mock-up and the field tests cost a few percent of the wall. One repeated defect costs several times that.

Worked example: the energy cost of air leakage

Air leakage in a hot-humid climate carries both heat and moisture, and removing moisture is a large share of the cooling load. Hypothetically, suppose a leaky envelope adds 15 percent to a building's cooling and dehumidification energy, and the building's annual cooling energy cost is 200,000 dollars. The leakage costs 30,000 dollars a year. If the owner pays common-area energy, or if high bills reduce the rent the market will pay, that is NOI. At a 6 percent cap rate, 30,000 dollars of NOI is worth 500,000 dollars of value. Leakage can also force larger cooling equipment, which costs capital at the start.

Worked example: life-cycle replacement

Sealants and roof membranes do not last as long as the building. A sealant joint might need replacement within a couple of decades, and a roof membrane on a similar cycle, depending on product and exposure. A capital reserve that ignores them overstates cash flow. Hypothetically, if resealing the whole building costs 300,000 dollars every 20 years, the reserve should set aside about 15,000 dollars a year in today's money, before inflation and the cost of access equipment. An envelope designed for easy access to joints and with durable materials lowers that number for the life of the asset.

How the best do it

Owners and contractors with strong envelope records commonly follow a sequence: a building enclosure consultant engaged in design, a performance mock-up built and tested before any production installation, the first installed areas tested as a benchmark, and periodic field testing through the job, often under a building enclosure commissioning process described by ASTM E2813; confirm the current edition. A small developer can copy the core of it cheaply: one consultant, one tested mock-up, and a rule that production does not begin until the mock-up passes.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet: envelope defects are a contingent liability that can surface years after you think a project is finished, and in a condominium they can come back to you through warranty and defect claims. Keep the test records, the consultant's reports and the warranties, and ask a licensed adviser how latent-defect exposure on completed projects should be carried on your own balance sheet and insured.

Worked example: the condominium warranty claim

In a condominium the arithmetic changes shape, because the owner of the claim is an owners' association and the defendant is often the developer. Hypothetically, a building of 80 units develops leaks at balcony door thresholds in its second year. The association's engineer estimates repair at 900,000 dollars, plus investigation and legal costs. The developer has sold every unit and distributed the profit. Unless the contract with the builder, the builder's insurance and any warranty scheme pick up the cost, it comes back to the developer's company, and if there were personal guarantees or a thin company, possibly further. A project that earned a hypothetical 3,000,000 dollar profit loses almost a third of it to one detail. The control is the same: the threshold detail tested on the mock-up, and the record kept.

There is also a sales cost. A building known for leaks resells at a discount, which buyers of your next project will hear about. Reputation is not on the balance sheet, but it is in your next absorption rate.

A lender will read the envelope lines the same way. A monitor who sees a tested mock-up and a field testing programme in the budget has one less reason to hold back contingency or ask for extra completion security, and an insurer underwriting latent-defect cover may ask for the same evidence.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is cutting the enclosure consultant, the mock-up or the field testing in value engineering because they look like soft costs, while the defects they prevent cost several times as much and arrive after the warranty clock has started. The control is to treat them as risk controls in the budget, with a line that cannot be moved without the owner's written decision.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares envelope bids on rate per square foot. Two bids that both exclude the junctions are both incomplete. Read the scope at windows, slab edges and roof edges before comparing prices.

Callback

In Week 14, Sage taught that stabilised NOI must carry realistic operating costs and reserves. Envelope energy and life-cycle replacement are exactly the costs a hopeful pro forma leaves out, and leaving them out overstates value by their capitalised amount.

Recap

The envelope is a large tender package, but its real cost includes leaks, mould, energy and replacement. A few percent of the wall cost on a consultant, a tested mock-up and field testing prevents defects that can cost several times as much. Air leakage and life-cycle replacement belong in NOI and the reserve.

Next: Ivo on The Rules: what the code and standards require of walls, roofs and windows, and how field tests are specified.
checklist: My envelope budget includes an enclosure consultant, a tested mock-up and field testing.
Those lines cannot be cut without my written decision.
I read each bid's scope at windows, slab edges and roof edges.
I know the cooling and dehumidification cost of air leakage.
My capital reserve carries sealant and roof replacement.
Production does not start until the mock-up passes its tests.
I keep envelope test records and warranties with the asset file.
head: Field checklist
speak: The envelope is priced at tender and paid for over its life. In a hypothetical case, a 5,400,000 dollar wall package needed only about 260,000 dollars, under 5 percent, for an enclosure consultant, a tested full-size mock-up and field testing during construction. One repeated window flashing defect without those controls cost about 700,000 dollars in repairs, consultants, legal costs and lost rent. Air leakage in a hot-humid climate adds cooling and dehumidification cost; 30,000 dollars a year is worth about 500,000 dollars of value at a 6 percent cap rate. And sealants and roof membranes need replacement long before the building ends, so the reserve must carry them. The best owners engage an enclosure consultant early, test a mock-up before production and keep testing through the job. I treat those as risk controls that cannot be cut without my written decision.
terms: Performance mock-up — a full-size sample of the wall or window system, built and tested for water and air before production installation.
Building enclosure commissioning — a quality process that verifies the envelope design and installation meet the owner's performance requirements.
Capital reserve — money set aside from operating income to replace building components as they wear out.

hostile.q: Your envelope budget carries 260,000 dollars for a consultant, a mock-up and testing. The contractor says his installers are experienced. Why not cut it?
hostile.a: Because experience does not test a junction, and the defects these controls prevent cost several times as much and appear after the warranty clock has started. A single repeated window defect could cost us around 700,000 dollars in repairs and lost rent. The mock-up also protects the contractor, because it settles the installation standard before production. I will keep the line, and I will share the mock-up results with you.

title: What the Code Asks of Walls, Roofs and Windows, and How Testing Is Specified
summary: The building code sets minimum requirements for weather protection, flashing, vapour retarders, roofs and the fire behaviour of exterior walls; the energy code adds air barriers and window performance. Field testing is mostly a contract matter: the code rarely requires it, so the owner must specify it. Name the standard, the pass criterion and who pays for a retest.
body:
The codes set minimum requirements for the envelope, but most of the testing that actually finds defects is required by contract, not by code. If you want it, you have to specify it: the standard, the pressure, the pass criterion and who pays when a test fails.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 103?

A. Never let a structural member or connection change after design without the engineer of record confirming in writing that the whole load path still works; a shop drawing stamp is not that confirmation.

Q. Who is the authority having jurisdiction?

A. The official or body, such as the building official or fire marshal, that interprets and enforces the code for a project.

Q. Why is dying without an estate plan a wealth failure?

A. Because the law then decides who inherits and who manages assets, often slowly and expensively, and the result may not match what the person wanted. Verify how intestacy works in each jurisdiction against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a wall leaks after completion, the first argument is about what the contract and the code required. A contractor will say the wall met code. That may be true and still leave you with a leaking wall, because the code sets a floor, and inspections during construction rarely test for water or air. This lesson teaches the structure of the rules and the contract terms that fill the gap. It is not legal advice and it is not a design.

What the building code covers

In plain English, the International Building Code (IBC), as adopted and amended locally, has a chapter on exterior walls and a chapter on roof assemblies. The exterior wall chapter requires a weather-resistant barrier behind most claddings, flashing at openings and at wall-to-roof and other intersections, and limits on vapour retarders by climate zone, with classes of vapour retarder defined by how much vapour they let through [unverified — confirm independently]. It also controls combustible materials in exterior walls of certain construction types, including the large-scale fire test of the wall assembly, NFPA 285, as Ford explained on Day 2. The roof chapter sets requirements for roof coverings, slopes, drainage, wind resistance and fire classification. Verify against the current adopted edition before you rely on any provision.

What the energy code adds

The energy code, either the International Energy Conservation Code or ASHRAE 90.1 as adopted, sets requirements for insulation, window U-factor and solar heat gain, and a continuous air barrier, the layer that stops air flowing through the envelope. Depending on the edition and path chosen, the air barrier may be shown to comply by materials, by tested assemblies such as those to ASTM E2357, or by a whole-building air leakage test [unverified — confirm independently]. Windows are commonly rated to the North American Fenestration Standard, AAMA/WDMA/CSA 101/I.S.2/A440, which sets performance grades for air, water and structural loading in the laboratory.

What field testing standards exist

Laboratory ratings tell you what a product can do; field tests tell you what the installation does. Common field standards include ASTM E1105, for water penetration of installed windows, doors and curtain walls under air pressure; AAMA 501.2, a nozzle spray check of joints and seals; ASTM E783, for air leakage of installed windows and doors; ASTM E779 or ASTM E3158, for whole-building air leakage; and, for roofs and waterproofing, methods such as flood testing and electronic leak detection [unverified — confirm independently]. Confirm the current edition of each before you write it into a specification.

Say that out loud now.

The code sets a floor. The testing that finds leaks is in my contract only if I put it there.

Worked example: the test clause that meant nothing

Hypothetically, a specification says: "Windows shall be field tested for water penetration." The contractor tests three windows of its choice at a low pressure, they pass, and the testing is complete. Later, leaks appear at windows near the roof, where wind pressure is highest. Nothing in the specification required otherwise.

A useful clause names the standard and edition, the test pressure as a stated fraction of the window's rated water test pressure, the number and location of tests chosen by the owner's consultant, the timing, including the first installations before production continues, the pass criterion, what happens on a failure, such as testing additional units, and who pays for retesting. Each element closes a gap the weak clause left open.

Worked example: the air barrier with no pass mark

Hypothetically, the drawings show a continuous air barrier, and the energy code compliance path requires a whole-building air leakage test. The specification does not say who conducts the test, when, or what happens if the result exceeds the target. The test is left to the end, the building fails, and the remedy, finding and sealing leaks behind finished drywall, is slow and disputed. The control is a clause that names the test, the target, an interim test of the air barrier before it is covered, and the contractor's duty to find and correct leaks at its own cost if the target is missed.

Warranties and the limitation clock

Envelope systems often carry manufacturers' warranties that require installation by approved installers and inspection by the manufacturer. A roof warranty may be void if another trade later penetrates the roof without the manufacturer's approved repair. Separately, the law limits how long after completion a defect claim can be brought; those periods vary by jurisdiction and by the type of claim. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it, and diarise the dates.

Worked example: the roof penetration that voided the warranty

Hypothetically, a roofing contractor installs a membrane and the manufacturer issues a long-term warranty after its inspection. Three months later, the mechanical contractor cuts two new curbs for rooftop units and flashes them himself. A leak appears the next winter at one curb. The manufacturer declines the claim because the penetrations were not made by an approved installer to its details. The owner now has a leak, no warranty for that area and an argument between two trades.

The control is a clause in every trade contract that no penetration of a warranted roof or wall is made without the warranting manufacturer's approved installer and details, and a pre-final walk of the roof with the manufacturer's representative after all trades have finished, not before.

One more rule of thumb: every field test in the specification should produce a dated report naming the tester, the standard, the pressure and the result, sent to the owner, the architect and the enclosure consultant at the same time. A test you cannot later produce is, in any dispute, a test that did not happen.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming that a wall that met code and passed inspection is a wall that does not leak. The control is a specification that names each field test, its standard, its pressure, its sample and its pass criterion, with testing at the first installations and the duty to retest at the contractor's cost on failure.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner relies on the window manufacturer's laboratory rating. A laboratory rating describes the window, not the hole in the wall it sits in. Test the installation.

Callback

In Week 78, LEX taught that risk allocation lives in the precise words of a clause: who bears the risk, on what trigger, up to what limit. A field testing clause is a risk allocation clause. Its pressure, sample and retest terms decide whether a leak is the contractor's problem during construction or yours after completion.

Recap

The building code sets minimums for weather barriers, flashing, vapour retarders, roofs and the fire behaviour of exterior walls; the energy code adds air barriers and window performance. Field testing is mostly a contract matter, so specify the standard, pressure, sample, timing, pass criterion and retest cost.

Professional sign-off required: architect of record; building enclosure consultant, for test specifications; lawyer, for warranty and limitation terms.

Next: Zara on The Numbers: reverse engineering a mould claim to its dew point and air leakage.
checklist: I know the adopted editions of the building and energy codes.
I know which compliance path the project uses for the air barrier.
Every field test names its standard and edition.
Test pressure, sample size and locations are set by the owner's consultant.
The first installations are tested before production continues.
The pass criterion and the retest cost on failure are in the contract.
The air barrier is tested before it is covered.
Warranty conditions and limitation dates are diarised.
head: Field checklist
speak: The building code, as adopted, sets minimums for the envelope: weather-resistant barriers, flashing at openings and intersections, vapour retarder limits by climate, roof coverings and drainage, and the fire behaviour of exterior walls, including NFPA 285 testing of assemblies with combustible components. The energy code adds a continuous air barrier and window performance. But inspections rarely test for water or air, so the testing that actually finds leaks is in my contract only if I put it there. I specify ASTM E1105 or AAMA 501.2 for installed windows, air leakage tests for the building, and methods for roofs, each with the standard and edition, the test pressure, a sample chosen by my consultant, testing at the first installations, a pass criterion and retesting at the contractor's cost on failure. I also diarise warranty conditions and limitation periods, which vary by jurisdiction.
terms: Air barrier — the continuous layer of materials and joints that stops air flowing through the building envelope.
Weather-resistant barrier — a membrane or coating behind the cladding that sheds water that gets past the outer layer.
Field test — a test of installed work on site, as opposed to a laboratory rating of a product.

hostile.q: The specification says only 'windows shall be field tested'. The contractor tested three windows and they passed. Why are you asking for more?
hostile.a: Because that clause did not say which windows, at what pressure, when or what happens on failure, so three passes tell us very little. We are issuing a clarification under the contract: tests to ASTM E1105 at a stated fraction of the rated pressure, on units chosen by our enclosure consultant including those near the roof, and additional units tested on any failure. If the contract requires a change order for that scope, we will price it; it is cheaper than a leak claim.

title: Reverse Engineering a Mould Claim to Its Dew Point and Air Leakage
summary: Start from a finished outcome, mould behind the wallcovering in air-conditioned rooms, and work backward to the physics that produced it: outdoor dew point, interior surface temperature, the leakage path and the trapping layer. Then reverse engineer a failed air leakage test to see how far the envelope missed its target. Each number points to a different repair.
body:
Mould behind a wall is the end of a chain of numbers: how humid the outside air is, how cold the inside surface is, how much air leaks in and what stops the wall drying. Work backward from the stain and you find which link to fix.

Recall

Q. What are the four control layers of the envelope, in order of importance?

A. Liquid water, air, water vapour and heat.

Q. What did reverse engineering a fire pump and tank quote reveal last fortnight?

A. That dividing tank volume by pump flow gave an implied duration far longer than the stated design duration, and that the demand-based tank was a fraction of the quoted one; the gap became a list of questions.

Q. What is intestacy?

A. Dying without a valid will, so that the law decides who inherits. Verify how it works in each jurisdiction against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even week, so we reverse engineer: start from a finished outcome and work backward. When an envelope fails, the first instinct is to blame the last trade that touched it. The arithmetic below tells you where the moisture came from and what kept it there, which decides both the repair and who should pay. Every temperature, humidity and leakage figure is a hypothetical round number chosen to teach the method. The real analysis needs a building enclosure consultant and, often, a hygrothermal model.

The outcome you are handed

A hypothetical apart-hotel in a hot-humid coastal climate reports mould on the back of vinyl wallcovering on exterior walls, worst on the windward side and on upper floors. The rooms are cooled to 72 degrees Fahrenheit. Your job is to explain why.

Step 1: the outdoor dew point

Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated. On a typical hypothetical summer day, outdoor air is 90 degrees Fahrenheit at 70 percent relative humidity. Its dew point is about 79 degrees Fahrenheit, which you can read from a psychrometric chart or a dew point calculator. That means any surface the outdoor air touches that is cooler than about 79 degrees will collect condensation.

Step 2: the surface temperature it meets

The back of the gypsum board is cooled by the 72 degree room. Its temperature is close to the room temperature, say 74 degrees, because the wallcovering and board resist heat only a little. Seventy-four is five degrees below the outdoor air's dew point of 79. So any outdoor air that reaches the back of the board will deposit water there.

Say that out loud now.

If humid outdoor air reaches a surface colder than its dew point, water appears. The question is how the air got there.

Step 3: the path

Vapour diffusion through solid materials is usually slow. Air leakage carries far more moisture, so look for the leak first. The pattern points to it: worse on the windward side, where wind pressure pushes air in, and worse on upper floors, where stack and wind effects are larger. The likely path is a gap in the air barrier, often at slab edges or window perimeters, letting humid outdoor air into the stud cavity.

Quantify it roughly. Suppose a leak lets 10 cubic feet per minute of outdoor air into one room's wall cavity. Outdoor air at 90 degrees and 70 percent humidity carries roughly 0.021 pounds of water per pound of dry air, against roughly 0.018 pounds when it is cooled to the 74 degree surface and saturated, a difference of about 0.003 pounds per pound. Ten cubic feet per minute is about 0.75 pounds of air a minute, since air weighs about 0.075 pounds per cubic foot, so about 0.0023 pounds of water condenses each minute, or a little over 3 pounds of water a day. At about 8.34 pounds per gallon, that is nearly half a gallon a day in one wall, every humid day.

Step 4: what kept it there

Water in a wall is a problem only if it cannot leave. The vinyl wallcovering stops it drying into the room; the exterior layers, designed to keep rain out, also slow drying outward. The wall stays wet, and mould grows. That is the trapping layer, and it is a design decision.

Step 5: what the numbers say about the fix

Three numbers point to three repairs. The leak rate points to sealing the air barrier at slab edges and windows. The surface temperature below dew point points to keeping humid outdoor air away from cooled surfaces altogether, through air sealing and slight positive pressurisation with dehumidified air. The trapping layer points to replacing the vinyl with a vapour-permeable finish. Do only the cosmetic repair, new wallcovering, and the mould returns.

Second outcome: the failed air leakage test

Now a second finished outcome: a whole-building air leakage test reports 60,000 cubic feet per minute at a test pressure of 75 pascals. The envelope area, all walls, roof and lowest floor, is 100,000 square feet. Divide: 60,000 divided by 100,000 equals 0.60 cubic feet per minute per square foot at 75 pascals.

Suppose the project's target, set in the specification or the compliance path, is 0.40 [unverified — confirm independently]. The building leaks 50 percent more than the target. Work backward to the gap: the target allows 0.40 times 100,000, or 40,000 cubic feet per minute, so 20,000 cubic feet per minute of leakage must be found and sealed. If smoke testing or infrared scanning shows the slab edges account for half of it, that tells the contractor where to start, and the retest will show whether it worked.

Step 6: who pays

The arithmetic informs the allocation. If the air barrier was drawn continuous and installed with gaps, that is installation. If the drawings never showed how it crossed the slab edge, that is design. If the wallcovering was a value-engineering substitution, that is a substitution decision. Each answer points to a different party and a different clause.

Checking the reverse calculation forward

Good reverse engineering ends by running the logic forward to see whether it reproduces what you observed. If the leak path is at slab edges on the windward side, the forward prediction is that rooms on the leeward side, or with tight slab edges, should be dry, and that the damage should be worst after long humid spells rather than after rainstorms. If the site shows mould on the leeward side too, or after storms only, the explanation is incomplete, and rain entry or an internal source such as a leaking condensate line must be investigated as well. The numbers tell you where to look; the pattern tells you whether you have found it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is repairing the symptom, the stain, without fixing the moisture source and the trapping layer, so the problem returns after the warranty period. The control is a forensic investigation by an enclosure consultant that identifies the path, the surface temperature and the trapping layer before any repair is designed.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes mould means a roof or window leak, and looks for rainwater. In a hot-humid climate, the water often comes from humid air, with no rain involved at all.

Callback

In Week 82, Vera taught that contemporaneous records decide disputes. An envelope claim is decided by the mock-up test records, the field test reports and photographs of the air barrier before cover. Without them, the arithmetic above can show what happened but not who was responsible.

Recap

Outdoor air at 90 degrees and 70 percent humidity has a dew point of about 79 degrees; a surface at 74 collects water from any of it that leaks in; ten cubic feet per minute can condense nearly half a gallon a day; vinyl traps it. A test of 0.60 against a target of 0.40 means 20,000 cubic feet per minute to find. Fix the path, the pressure and the trap, not the stain.

Professional sign-off required: building enclosure consultant, for the forensic investigation; mechanical engineer, for pressurisation and dehumidification.

Next: Zara in The Room: the mock-up test fails and the contractor wants to start production anyway.
checklist: I start an envelope investigation from the outdoor dew point.
I compare the dew point with the interior surface temperature.
I look for an air leakage path before blaming diffusion or rain.
I identify the layer that stops the wall drying.
I divide measured leakage by envelope area and compare with the target.
I know how much leakage must be found to meet the target.
I allocate responsibility by design, installation or substitution.
I never accept a cosmetic repair for a moisture problem.
head: Field checklist
speak: When mould appears behind wallcovering in air-conditioned rooms, I work backward. In a hypothetical case, outdoor air at 90 degrees Fahrenheit and 70 percent humidity has a dew point of about 79 degrees. The back of the drywall in a 72 degree room is about 74, so any outdoor air that reaches it deposits water. The pattern, worse on the windward side and upper floors, points to air leaking through gaps in the air barrier, at slab edges and windows. Ten cubic feet per minute of leakage can condense nearly half a gallon a day in one wall. The vinyl wallcovering stops it drying. So the repair is to seal the air barrier, pressurise with dry air and use a permeable finish, not just replace the vinyl. For a failed air leakage test, I divide measured flow by envelope area, compare with the target and calculate how much leakage must be found.
terms: Relative humidity — the amount of water vapour in air as a percentage of the most it could hold at that temperature.
Psychrometric chart — a chart relating air temperature, humidity, dew point and moisture content, used to analyse condensation.
Hygrothermal model — a computer analysis of how heat and moisture move through an assembly over time.

hostile.q: You want the contractor to pay for mould repairs in 40 rooms. He says the wallcovering was your substitution. Why is it his problem?
hostile.a: It may be partly ours, and the analysis is designed to tell us. The moisture comes from humid air leaking through gaps in the air barrier at slab edges, which the drawings show as continuous and the field photographs show were not sealed; that is installation. The vinyl stopped the wall drying, and if it was our substitution, we carry that part. I propose we share the investigation report and allocate cost by cause, rather than argue over the whole.

title: The Mock-up Fails and the Contractor Wants to Start Production
summary: A site meeting after the performance mock-up fails its water test. The contractor wants to start production installation to protect the schedule and fix the detail as it goes. The scene gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question and when to stay silent. The goal is a fixed, retested detail before production, with the schedule protected another way.
body:
A failed mock-up is good news that feels like bad news. It found the defect on one panel instead of four hundred. The owner's job in the meeting is to keep that advantage by refusing production until the fixed detail passes, while helping the contractor protect the schedule.

Recall

Q. What does a measured air leakage of 0.60 against a target of 0.40 tell you?

A. That the building leaks 50 percent more than the target, and that the leakage to be found equals the difference times the envelope area.

Q. What was the root cause of the Grenfell Tower envelope failure, from an owner's seat?

A. A combustible exterior was installed because every party relied on someone else's paper instead of proven performance of the whole assembly as built.

Q. In the fire marshal meeting, what do you leave with?

A. The evidence the authority wants, any peer review arrangement, the review timeline and the likely conditions, confirmed in a written summary.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the most valuable sentence in envelope quality control is "the mock-up failed". The most expensive sentence is "we will fix it in production". Between them sits a meeting where the contractor has real schedule pressure, the installers are mobilised and the windows are on site. How you handle it decides whether a defect is fixed once or repeated hundreds of times.

The scene

A hypothetical residential building's performance mock-up, a full-size section of wall with two windows, a slab edge and a corner, has been tested for water penetration. Water appeared on the interior at one window's lower corner under the test pressure. The enclosure consultant attributes it to a sill pan joint and a gap in the air barrier transition. Present are the contractor's project manager, the window installer, the air barrier installer, the architect, the enclosure consultant, your owner's representative and you.

The opening

You speak first: "Thank you all. The mock-up has done its job; it found a problem while it is still one panel. We are not going to start production until a revised detail passes a retest. What I want from this meeting is the revised detail, who owns each part of it, and the fastest way to retest. I also want to hear how we protect the schedule while we do that."

Then stop. You have set the boundary and invited the solution in one breath.

Say that out loud now.

The mock-up found it on one panel. We fix it and retest before we build four hundred.

The question behind the question

The contractor's project manager says: "We can start on the north elevation and apply the fix as we learn." On the surface that is a schedule proposal. The question behind it is who will carry the cost of delay. If you say no without engaging, you are telling the contractor the delay is his alone, and he will look for ways to recover it from you.

The answer that holds the line and engages: "Production does not start before a pass. But let's look at what can move. Can we resequence to work that does not depend on this detail, such as roofing or interior rough-in? Can the retest be arranged within days rather than weeks if I authorise the consultant's time now? And if the cause turns out to be a design gap, we will discuss the time and cost under the contract." That separates the safety boundary from the commercial question.

Lines never to say

Never say "just make sure it doesn't leak". It sets no standard and transfers nothing. Never say "it was only one window". In production it is every window. Never assign blame between the window installer and the air barrier installer in the room; the junction is exactly the place where each will point at the other. Your line instead: "Who owns the joint between the sill pan and the air barrier? I want one name."

When to stay silent

When the enclosure consultant explains the failure, do not interrupt, even if the contractor does. Ask the contractor to let the consultant finish. Then let a pause follow. The installers will often say, in that pause, the thing nobody put in a report, such as "we never had the transition membrane on site for the mock-up".

Holding your state

A schedule threat is designed to make you feel the delay in your stomach. Notice it, and remember that the cost of a repeated defect is far larger than a short delay. Speak slower than the contractor. Write down each proposed change to the detail exactly as said; precise notes keep the conversation technical.

Working with advisers

This month's thread is how you use advisers. Your enclosure consultant is paid to tell you the truth about the wall, and in this meeting their authority must be visible. Back them in front of the contractor, and challenge them in private. Ask them before the meeting what result would change their view, and after it whether anything in the room should change their recommendation.

The trap runs the other way too. An adviser who knows you want speed may soften their finding. Tell them at engagement that you want the uncomfortable answer early, and reward it when you get it. An adviser you only hear agreeing with you is an adviser you are not using.

The outcome to leave with

Leave with a revised detail sketched and assigned, one named owner for each junction, a retest date, a resequenced short-term programme, and a note that the cause, design or installation, will be determined and handled under the contract. Send it in writing within 24 hours.

The second voice: the installer who disagrees

The window installer says: "We installed it exactly per the manufacturer's detail." That may be true, and it does not settle the matter, because the manufacturer's detail may not show how its sill pan joins this project's air barrier. Your line: "I believe you. The failure is at the joint between your scope and the air barrier. I want the architect and the consultant to draw that joint for this wall, and I want both installers to agree it before the retest." That moves the conversation from defence to design, and it gives the junction an owner.

When the revised detail is drawn, ask for it to be added to the drawings formally, by sketch or bulletin, so that the detail the installers follow in production is the one that passed, and the record shows when it changed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting production start before the fixed detail passes, so a defect found once is built hundreds of times. The control is a written rule, agreed at the start of the envelope package, that production of each system begins only after its mock-up passes, with resequencing used to protect the schedule.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sees the failed mock-up as a setback and looks for someone to blame. It is the cheapest defect the project will ever have. Treat it as a success of the process and spend the meeting on the fix.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya and Ford taught that a draw must never run ahead of verified work in place, because cash spent ahead of proof is the hardest money to recover. Production ahead of a passed mock-up is the same error in the envelope: commitment running ahead of proof, with the cost of reversing it growing every day.

Recap

Celebrate the failure as a defect found on one panel, refuse production until a revised detail passes, separate the safety boundary from the commercial question, name one owner for every junction, let the consultant finish and the installers fill the pause, and leave with a written plan and a retest date.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: Week 104 review, with Cole in the Auditor's Chair.
checklist: I treat a failed mock-up as a defect found cheaply.
No production starts until the revised detail passes a retest.
I offer resequencing to protect the schedule.
I separate the safety boundary from the commercial question of who pays.
I name one owner for every junction between trades.
I let the enclosure consultant finish without interruption.
I back my consultant in the room and challenge them in private.
I send a written plan with a retest date within 24 hours.
head: Field checklist
speak: When the performance mock-up fails its water test, I call it what it is: a defect found on one panel instead of four hundred. I open by saying production will not start until a revised detail passes a retest, and that I want the revised detail, one owner for each part of it, the fastest retest and a way to protect the schedule. When the contractor proposes starting production and fixing as we go, I hear the real question, who carries the delay, and I separate it from the safety boundary: no production before a pass, but let's resequence to unaffected work, authorise a quick retest, and handle cost under the contract once we know whether it is design or installation. I never say 'it was only one window'. I ask for one name for the sill pan to air barrier joint. I back my consultant in the room and leave with a written plan and retest date.
terms: Production installation — installation of a system across the building after the mock-up has established the standard.
Resequencing — changing the order of work so that tasks not affected by a hold can proceed while it is resolved.
Transition membrane — a flexible membrane that joins one control layer to another, such as the air barrier to a window frame.

hostile.q: Every day we wait on the retest costs us 15,000 dollars in idle crew and equipment. Will you pay for it?
hostile.a: I will not pay for production that would repeat a known defect, but I will help you avoid the idle cost. I have authorised the consultant to retest within days, and I want your resequenced plan by tomorrow so crews move to work that does not depend on this detail. If the investigation shows the failure came from a design gap, we will deal with time and cost under the contract, and I will not hide from that.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 104 Review: The Envelope, With Cole in the Auditor's Chair
summary: Six questions test the week: the four control layers, hot-humid vapour drive, what the envelope really costs, what the code and contract require, reverse engineering a mould claim and the failed mock-up meeting. Cole takes the Auditor's Chair to read a hypothetical envelope closeout report as a hostile auditor would. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one idea: the envelope works only if every control layer is continuous through every junction, and the owner can know that only from tests of the assembly as built, specified in the contract and kept in the record.

Recall

Q. What is the most valuable sentence in envelope quality control?

A. The mock-up failed, because it finds a defect on one panel before it is repeated across the building.

Q. What is Rule 102?

A. Never let a fire strategy depend on the fire being found early; every space gets a layer that holds the fire on its own, and every vertical opening is sealed against smoke.

Q. What links the wealth post-mortems of currency mismatch, concentration and custody fraud?

A. Each is a single exposure that a balance sheet did not measure or control, so one event damaged the whole position; the defence is measurement, limits and independent verification.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the envelope is where your building meets the weather every day for decades, and where most post-completion claims begin. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the four control layers in order of importance.

Answer: Liquid water, air, water vapour and heat, each needing a continuous layer through every junction.

Question 2. Which way does the vapour drive in a hot-humid climate, and what follows?

Answer: Inward, from the hot, humid outside to the cooled inside. So keep the air barrier continuous, keep impermeable finishes off the interior face, let the wall dry inward and pressurise slightly with dry air.

Question 3. Why is an enclosure consultant, mock-up and field testing worth their cost?

Answer: They cost a few percent of the wall package and prevent repeated defects that can cost several times as much, arriving after the warranty clock has started, with lost rent and reputation on top.

Question 4. Who requires field testing of the envelope?

Answer: Mostly the contract, not the code. The owner must specify the standard and edition, pressure, sample, timing, pass criterion and who pays for retesting.

Question 5. How do you reverse engineer mould behind wallcovering?

Answer: Find the outdoor dew point, compare it with the interior surface temperature, find the air leakage path, and identify the layer that stops the wall drying. Fix the path, the pressure and the trap, not the stain.

Question 6. What is Rule 104?

Answer: Never accept an envelope product on a certificate or a component test; require proof that the whole assembly, as built, passes the governing fire test, and re-approve every substitution in writing.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Zara taught the four control layers and the inward vapour drive of a hot-humid climate. Ford and Cole took the Grenfell Tower fire of 2017, giving Rule 104. Sage priced the envelope over its life. Ivo set out what the codes require and what only the contract can require. Zara reverse engineered a mould claim and a failed air leakage test, then ran the failed mock-up meeting.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 104 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical envelope closeout report as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Envelope Closeout Report. 1. All windows comply with the manufacturer's laboratory rating; certificates attached. 2. Field water testing: five windows tested by the window installer, all passed. 3. Whole-building air leakage test: 0.55 cfm per square foot at 75 Pa; considered acceptable given building complexity. 4. Cladding panels: substituted for an equivalent product with the same certificate; no change to fire performance. 5. Interior finish on exterior walls: vinyl wallcovering per owner's value engineering. 6. Roof warranty issued; mechanical contractor added two curb penetrations after warranty inspection. 7. Air barrier inspected visually; no photographs retained.

The auditor's reading. First, item 1 relies on laboratory ratings, which describe the product, not the installation. Second, item 2 has the installer testing its own work, on windows apparently of its choosing, with no standard, pressure or locations stated. Third, item 3 reports a result above a typical target and calls it acceptable without stating the target, who accepted it or on what authority. Fourth, item 4 substitutes cladding on a certificate, with no test of the whole assembly and no written re-approval by the architect and fire protection engineer, which breaks Rule 104. Fifth, item 5 records an impermeable interior finish in what this week's lessons would treat as a hot-humid risk, with no moisture analysis. Sixth, item 6 describes roof penetrations made after the warranty inspection, which may have voided the warranty. Seventh, item 7 admits there is no photographic record of the air barrier before cover, so its continuity cannot be proven.

Then the auditor asks for evidence: the test reports with standards and pressures, the name of whoever accepted the air leakage result, the fire test of the substituted assembly, the moisture analysis for the wallcovering, the manufacturer's acceptance of the new roof penetrations, and the inspection photographs. That list is the real lesson. A closeout report is only as strong as the evidence behind each line.

Boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to a board about to accept the envelope at completion. Time yourself, then read the model answer.

Model answer: "Our envelope controls water, air, vapour and heat, and each layer has to be continuous through every junction. In this climate the vapour drives inward, so we kept impermeable finishes off the interior walls and pressurise the building with dry air. We tested a full-size mock-up before production and fixed the one failure it found. Our enclosure consultant chose the windows for field testing, including those near the roof, under stated standards and pressures, and our air leakage test met the contract target. Every envelope substitution was re-approved in writing, and the cladding assembly as built has a passing fire test. Our roof warranty is intact because every penetration was approved by the manufacturer. The test reports, photographs and warranties are in the asset file. Our rule is simple: we accept the envelope on tests of the assembly as built, not on certificates."

Scoring your drill

Record it on your phone and score it from 1 to 5 for accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question. For the hard question, imagine a board member asking: "Why not accept the 0.55 leakage result and move on?" A strong answer: "Because the contract sets the target, and a leakier envelope means higher cooling costs and moisture risk for the life of the building. The contractor finds and seals the leakage, then we retest."

Three confusions to clear up

First, a vapour retarder and an air barrier are not the same thing; one slows diffusion through materials, the other stops air moving through gaps, and in a hot-humid wall the second matters far more. Second, a laboratory window rating is not a field result; the installation is what leaks. Third, a passing mock-up is not a passing building; it sets the standard that production must then repeat, which is why field testing continues through the job.

And one habit for the week: next time it rains, look at the sill of any window you can reach and ask where water would go if it got past the frame. If you cannot see a path down and out, you have found the question to ask on your own projects.

Callback

In Week 83, Cole taught that an independent review is only as useful as its independence and scope. An installer testing his own windows is the envelope's version of a reviewer chosen by the person he reviews.

Recap

Know the four layers and the inward vapour drive, price the envelope over its life, specify field testing in the contract, reverse engineer moisture from dew point to trap, and refuse production until the mock-up passes. Accept the envelope on evidence of the assembly as built.

head: The six questions
speak: The envelope controls four things in order: liquid water, air, water vapour and heat, each with a continuous layer through every junction. In a hot-humid climate vapour drives inward, so I seal the air barrier, keep impermeable finishes off interior walls, let walls dry inward and pressurise with dry air. An enclosure consultant, a tested mock-up and field testing cost a few percent of the wall package and prevent defects that cost several times more after the warranty clock starts. The code sets minimums, but the testing that finds leaks is in my contract only if I specify it. I reverse engineer moisture from dew point to surface temperature to leakage path to the trapping layer. When the mock-up fails, production waits for a retest. Rule 104: never accept an envelope product on a certificate or a component test; require proof the whole assembly as built passes the governing fire test, and re-approve every substitution in writing.
terms: Closeout report — the record, delivered at completion, summarising tests, approvals, warranties and outstanding items for a building system.
Warranty inspection — a manufacturer's inspection of an installed system, such as a roof, which its warranty may require and later work may void.
Target leakage rate — the maximum air leakage per square foot of envelope at a stated test pressure, set in the specification or compliance path.

hostile.q: Your closeout report says the cladding was substituted for an equivalent with the same certificate. Prove to me the wall as built will not carry fire.
hostile.a: On what is in that report, I cannot, and I will not sign the envelope off until I can. I am asking the manufacturer for the governing fire test of the whole assembly as built, with our insulation, sheathing, cavity and fixings, and the architect and fire protection engineer for written re-approval. If that evidence does not exist, we will treat the substitution as non-conforming and agree a remedy with the contractor, including replacement if necessary.
